title: Wildlife strip planting on a smallholding
subtitle: Sowing a field margin or headland to attract insects, birds, and mammals.
excerpt: A wildlife strip is a sown or managed area of grass and wildflowers at the edge of a field or along an internal boundary. Even a 3-metre-wide strip around the outside of a 2-acre paddock adds over 1,000 m2 of habitat. The practical work is: stop mowing or grazing the strip, prepare the seedbed if needed, and choose the right seed mix for the soil and your target species.
sourceNotes: Buglife, Wildflower Strips: A Practical Guide (2022). Plantlife, Meadow Creation Guidance (2021). RSPB, Farming for Wildlife: Field Margins (2022).

glossaryTerms.definition: A blend of grass and native flowering plant seeds chosen to create diverse, low-fertility habitat. Mix composition varies by soil type and target species.
The annual or biennial cutting regime that prevents coarse grasses from dominating a wildflower strip and removes accumulated thatch.

content.text: A wildlife strip creates a transition zone between managed land (pasture, hay meadow, vegetable plot) and a field boundary hedge or fence. The zone gives ground-nesting birds undisturbed cover, bees and hoverflies a foraging area, and barn owls a hunting corridor. The most important thing is to stop the routine management: the stopping is the planting.
A 3-metre strip is the minimum useful width. 6 metres produces measurably better invertebrate diversity. On very small holdings, a 1.5-metre strip is still worth doing.
Place strips along existing hedges, stream banks, and fence lines to extend existing habitat corridors. Isolated strips in the middle of a paddock are less valuable than connected ones.
South or southwest-facing edges are the most valuable for invertebrates. A sun-warmed strip of bare earth and open flowers in this aspect is used intensively by solitary bees.
Preparing the seedbed for a new strip
On improved pasture or amenity grass, rye-grass and clover will crowd out most wildflowers if the ground is not prepared first.
Remove fertility: do not add any fertiliser or manure to the strip. Wildflowers favour low-fertility, slightly acidic to neutral soils. High fertility gives rank grass.
Strim very short (below 5 cm), then scarify with a garden rake or a drag harrow to create bare patches. Sow into the bare patches at the rate on the
label (typically 2 to 4 g per m2). Brush seed into contact with soil without burying deep; wildflower seeds need light to germinate.

A wildlife strip needs one cut per year in late summer (August to September) to prevent scrub encroachment and remove the accumulated thatch. Cut to 10 to 15 cm, remove the cuttings (leaving them in situ mulches the soil and enriches it, encouraging rank grass). Leave 20% of the strip uncut each year as a winter refuge for overwintering invertebrates; rotate the uncut section each season.

attrs.title: On land already receiving Countryside Stewardship payments

content.text: If you have a CS agreement including AB8 (flower-rich margins and plots) or AB15 (two-year legume fallow), your management obligations are already set by the option management requirements. Do not deviate from the cutting regime or add seed mixes not specified in the option without checking with your Natural England adviser.

attrs.cue: Strip dominated by docks and nettles after stopping mowing
attrs.cause: High-fertility soil or disturbed bare ground favouring competitive ruderal plants
attrs.fix: Cut the nettles and docks short in May before they set seed. Dig out dock taproots individually where possible. Sow yellow rattle (Rhinanthus minor) seed in autumn: it parasitises grass roots and opens the sward for wildflowers without the need for expensive seedbed preparation.

attrs.cue: No wildflower germination despite sowing at the correct rate
attrs.cause: Seed buried too deep, sown too late in the season, or soil fertility too high for the species in the mix
attrs.fix: Wildflower seed can take 2 to 3 years to fully establish. Yellow rattle tends to show in year 2 once the sward opens. If nothing is showing by year 2, resow in August into lightly scarified areas with a species suited to your soil type.
